### Central banking in the United States, 1791–1913

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federal_Reserve&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: Central banking in the United States, 1791–1913")]

The first attempt at a national currency was during the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). In 1775, the Continental Congress, as well as the states, began issuing paper currency, calling the bills "[Continentals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_American_currency "Early American currency")".[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-131) The Continentals were backed only by future tax revenue, and were used to help finance the Revolutionary War. Overprinting, as well as British counterfeiting, caused the value of the Continental to diminish quickly. This experience with paper money led the United States to strip the power to issue Bills of Credit (paper money) from a draft of the new Constitution on August 16, 1787,[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-132) as well as banning such issuance by the various states, and limiting the states' ability to make anything but gold or silver coin legal tender on August 28.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-133)

In 1791, the government granted the [First Bank of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bank_of_the_United_States "First Bank of the United States") a charter to operate as the U.S. central bank until 1811.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-A_Brief_History_of_Our_Nation's_Paper_Money-134) The First Bank of the United States came to an end under [President Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Madison "President Madison") when Congress refused to renew its charter. The [Second Bank of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bank_of_the_United_States "Second Bank of the United States") was established in 1816, and lost its authority to be the central bank of the U.S. twenty years later under [President Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Jackson "President Jackson") when its charter expired. Both banks were based upon the Bank of England.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-135) Ultimately, a third national bank, known as the Federal Reserve, was established in 1913 and still exists to this day.

#### First Central Bank, 1791 and Second Central Bank, 1816

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federal_Reserve&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: First Central Bank, 1791 and Second Central Bank, 1816")]

The first U.S. institution with central banking responsibilities was the [First Bank of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bank_of_the_United_States "First Bank of the United States"), chartered by Congress and signed into law by President [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on February 25, 1791, at the urging of [Alexander Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton "Alexander Hamilton"). This was done despite strong opposition from [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") and [James Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison "James Madison"), among numerous others. The charter was for twenty years and expired in 1811 under President Madison, when Congress refused to renew it.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-boshistory-136)

In 1816, however, Madison revived it in the form of the [Second Bank of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bank_of_the_United_States "Second Bank of the United States"). Years later, early renewal of the bank's charter became the primary issue in the reelection of President [Andrew Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Jackson "Andrew Jackson"). After Jackson, who was opposed to the central bank, was reelected, he pulled the government's funds out of the bank. Jackson was the only President to completely pay off the national debt[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-137) but his efforts to close the bank contributed to the [Panic of 1837](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1837 "Panic of 1837"). The bank's charter was not renewed in 1836, and it would fully dissolve after several years as a private corporation.

From 1837 to 1862, in the [Free Banking Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Banking_Era "Free Banking Era") there was no formal central bank. From 1846 to 1921, an [Independent Treasury System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_Treasury_System "Independent Treasury System") ruled. From 1863 to 1913, a system of national banks was instituted by the 1863 [National Banking Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Banking_Act "National Banking Act") during which a series of bank panics, in [1873](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1873 "Panic of 1873"), [1893](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1893 "Panic of 1893"), and [1907](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907 "Panic of 1907") occurred.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-FDS-H-04-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-FDS-H-05-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-FDS-H-06-10)

#### Creation of Third Central Bank, 1907–1913

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federal_Reserve&action=edit&section=41 "Edit section: Creation of Third Central Bank, 1907–1913")]

The main motivation for the third central banking system came from the [Panic of 1907](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1907 "Panic of 1907"), which caused a renewed desire among legislators, economists, and bankers for an overhaul of the monetary system.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-FDS-H-04-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-FDS-H-05-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-FDS-H-06-10)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-herrickpanic-138) During the last quarter of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century, the United States economy went through a series of [financial panics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_panics "Financial panics").[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-EFlaherty-139) According to many economists, the previous national banking system had two main weaknesses: an [inelastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inelastic "Inelastic") currency and a lack of liquidity.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-EFlaherty-139) In 1908, Congress enacted the [Aldrich–Vreeland Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldrich%E2%80%93Vreeland_Act "Aldrich–Vreeland Act"), which provided for an emergency currency and established the [National Monetary Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Monetary_Commission "National Monetary Commission") to study banking and currency reform.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-mnwarburg-140) The National Monetary Commission returned with recommendations which were repeatedly rejected by Congress. A revision crafted during a secret meeting on [Jekyll Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jekyll_Island "Jekyll Island") by Senator Aldrich and representatives of the nation's top finance and industrial groups later became the basis of the [Federal Reserve Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act "Federal Reserve Act").[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-141)

##### Federal Reserve Act, 1913

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federal_Reserve&action=edit&section=42 "Edit section: Federal Reserve Act, 1913")]

[![Image 21](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Fed_Reserve.JPG/500px-Fed_Reserve.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fed_Reserve.JPG)

Newspaper clipping, December 24, 1913

The head of the bipartisan National Monetary Commission was financial expert and Senate [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") leader [Nelson Aldrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Aldrich "Nelson Aldrich"). Aldrich set up two commissions – one to study the American monetary system in depth and the other, headed by Aldrich himself, to study the European central banking systems and report on them.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-mnwarburg-140)

In early November 1910, Aldrich met with five well known members of the New York banking community to devise a central banking bill. [Paul Warburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Warburg "Paul Warburg"), an attendee of the meeting and longtime advocate of central banking in the U.S., later wrote that Aldrich was "bewildered at all that he had absorbed abroad and he was faced with the difficult task of writing a highly technical bill while being harassed by the daily grind of his parliamentary duties".[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-Warburg_document-142) After ten days of deliberation, the bill, which would later be referred to as the "Aldrich Plan", was agreed upon. It had several key components, including a central bank with a Washington-based headquarters and fifteen branches located throughout the U.S. in geographically strategic locations, and a uniform elastic currency based on gold and commercial paper. Aldrich believed a central banking system with no political involvement was best, but was convinced by Warburg that a plan with no public control was not politically feasible.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-Warburg_document-142) The compromise involved representation of the public sector on the board of directors.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-ecresearch-143)

Aldrich's bill met much opposition from politicians. Critics charged Aldrich of being biased due to his close ties to wealthy bankers such as [J. P. Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._P._Morgan "J. P. Morgan") and [John D. Rockefeller Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_D._Rockefeller_Jr. "John D. Rockefeller Jr."), Aldrich's son-in-law. Most Republicans favored the Aldrich Plan,[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-ecresearch-143) but it lacked enough support in Congress to pass because rural and western states viewed it as favoring the "eastern establishment".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-mnglass-5)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-144) In contrast, progressive Democrats favored a reserve system owned and operated by the government; they believed that public ownership of the central bank would end Wall Street's control of the American currency supply.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-ecresearch-143) Conservative Democrats fought for a privately owned, yet decentralized, reserve system, which would still be free of Wall Street's control.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-ecresearch-143)

The original Aldrich Plan was dealt a fatal blow in 1912, when Democrats won the White House and Congress.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-Warburg_document-142) Nonetheless, President [Woodrow Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson "Woodrow Wilson") believed that the Aldrich plan would suffice with a few modifications. The plan became the basis for the Federal Reserve Act, which was proposed by Senator [Robert Owen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_L._Owen "Robert L. Owen") in May 1913. The primary difference between the two bills was the transfer of control of the board of directors (called the Federal Open Market Committee in the Federal Reserve Act) to the government.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-mnglass-5)[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-boshistory-136) The bill passed Congress on December 23, 1913,[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-145) on a mostly partisan basis, with most Democrats voting "yea" and most Republicans voting "nay".[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-boshistory-136)

The House voted on December 22, 1913, with 298 voting yes to 60 voting no. The Senate voted 43–25 on December 23, 1913.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-146) President [Woodrow Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson "Woodrow Wilson") signed the bill later that day.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-147)

The most common measures are named M0 (narrowest), M1, M2, and M3. In the United States they are defined by the Federal Reserve as follows:

### Personal consumption expenditures price index

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federal_Reserve&action=edit&section=48 "Edit section: Personal consumption expenditures price index")]

The [personal consumption expenditures price index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_consumption_expenditures_price_index "Personal consumption expenditures price index"), also referred to as simply the PCE price index, is used as one measure of the value of money. It is a United States-wide indicator of the average increase in prices for all domestic personal consumption. Using a variety of data including [United States Consumer Price Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Consumer_Price_Index "United States Consumer Price Index") and [U.S. Producer Price Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Producer_Price_Index "U.S. Producer Price Index") prices, it is derived from the largest component of the [gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") in the BEA's [National Income and Product Accounts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Income_and_Product_Accounts "National Income and Product Accounts"), personal consumption expenditures.

One of the Fed's main roles is to maintain price stability, which means that the Fed's ability to keep a low inflation rate is a long-term measure of their success.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-159) Although the Fed is not required to maintain inflation within a specific range, their long run target for the growth of the PCE price index is between 1.5 and 2 percent.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-160) There has been debate among policy makers as to whether the Federal Reserve should have a specific [inflation targeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation_targeting "Inflation targeting") policy.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-161)

#### Inflation and the economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federal_Reserve&action=edit&section=49 "Edit section: Inflation and the economy")]

Most [mainstream economists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainstream_economists "Mainstream economists") favor a low, steady rate of inflation.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-econjournalwatch.org-162)[Chief economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_economist "Chief economist"), and advisor to the Federal Reserve, the [Congressional Budget Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Budget_Office "Congressional Budget Office") and the [Council of Economic Advisers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Economic_Advisers "Council of Economic Advisers"),[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-163)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-164)[Diane C. Swonk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_C._Swonk "Diane C. Swonk") observed, in 2022, that "From the Fed's perspective, you have to remember inflation is kind of like cancer. If you don't deal with it now with something that may be painful, you could have something that metastasized and becomes much more chronic later on."[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-165)

Low (as opposed to zero or [negative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deflation "Deflation")) inflation may reduce the severity of economic [recessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recession "Recession") by enabling the labor market to adjust more quickly in a downturn, and reduce the risk that a [liquidity trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquidity_trap "Liquidity trap") prevents [monetary policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_policy "Monetary policy") from stabilizing the economy.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-166) The task of keeping the rate of inflation low and stable is usually given to [monetary authorities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_authority "Monetary authority").

[![Image 25](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/US_Seasonal_Unemployment.svg/500px-US_Seasonal_Unemployment.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:US_Seasonal_Unemployment.svg)

The Federal Reserve is self-funded. Over 90% of Fed revenues come from open market operations, specifically the interest on the portfolio of Treasury securities as well as "capital gains/losses" that may arise from the buying/selling of the securities and their derivatives as part of Open Market Operations. The balance of revenues come from sales of financial services (check and electronic payment processing) and discount window loans.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-167)

The Federal Reserve Board creates a budget report once per year for Congress. There are two reports with budget information. The one that lists the complete balance statements with income and expenses, as well as the net profit or loss, is the large report simply titled, "Annual Report". It also includes data about employment throughout the system. The other report, which explains in more detail the expenses of the different aspects of the whole system, is called "Annual Report: Budget Review".[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-budget-168)

The Federal Reserve has been [remitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remitting "Remitting") interest that it has been receiving back to the [United States Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Treasury "United States Treasury"). Most of the assets the Fed holds are [U.S. Treasury bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Treasury_security "United States Treasury security") and [mortgage-backed securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage-backed_securities "Mortgage-backed securities") that it has been purchasing as part of [quantitative easing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_easing "Quantitative easing") since the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"). In 2022, the Fed started [quantitative tightening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_tightening "Quantitative tightening") (QT) and selling these assets and taking a loss on them in the [secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_market "Secondary market")[bond market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bond_market "Bond market"). As a result, the nearly $100 billion that it was remitting annually to the Treasury, is expected to be discontinued during QT.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-169)[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-170)

In 2023, the Federal Reserve reported a net negative income of $114.3 billion.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-171) This triggered the creation of a deferred asset liability on the Federal Reserve balance sheet booked as "Interest on Federal Reserve notes due to U.S. Treasury" totaling $133.3 billion.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-172) The deferred asset is the amount of net excess revenues the Federal Reserve must realize before remittances can continue. It does not have any impact on the ability of the Federal Reserve to conduct monetary policy or meet its obligations.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-173) The Federal Reserve has estimated the deferred asset will last until mid-2027.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-174)

One of the keys to understanding the Federal Reserve is the Federal Reserve balance sheet (or [balance statement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balance_sheet "Balance sheet")). In accordance with Section 11 of the [Federal Reserve Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Act "Federal Reserve Act"), the [board of governors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_governors "Board of governors") of the Federal Reserve System publishes once each week the "Consolidated Statement of Condition of All Federal Reserve Banks" showing the condition of each Federal Reserve bank and a consolidated statement for all Federal Reserve banks. The board of governors requires that excess earnings of the Reserve Banks be transferred to the Treasury as interest on Federal Reserve notes.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-175)

The Federal Reserve System has faced various criticisms since its inception in 1913. Some of the most common critiques focus on its monetary policy, lack of transparency, and its potential role in exacerbating financial instability.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-bi-ronpaul-178) Critics argue that the Fed’s expansionary policies—such as lowering interest rates and increasing the money supply—can lead to inflation, asset bubbles, and economic distortions. Prominent economists like [Milton Friedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Friedman "Milton Friedman") have criticized the Fed for contributing to economic downturns, including its role in the Great Depression.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-:0-179) Economist [Hans Sennholz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Sennholz "Hans Sennholz") called the Fed's creation, "the most tragic blunder ever committed by Congress. The day it was passed, old America died and a new era began. A new institution was born that was to cause, or greatly contribute to, the unprecedented economic instability in the decades to come."[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-180)

[Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarianism_in_the_United_States "Libertarianism in the United States") figures such as [Ron Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Paul "Ron Paul") have been especially vocal in calling for greater accountability and transparency within the Fed, advocating for measures such as auditing the Federal Reserve to ensure it serves the public interest rather than benefiting large financial institutions. Additionally, some critics, including [Rand Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rand_Paul "Rand Paul"), argue that the Fed disproportionately serves the interests of the banking elite, given the backgrounds of many of its officials in finance and banking, leading to potential conflicts of interest and policies that favor [Wall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street "Wall Street") over the general economy.

Another area of criticism is the Federal Reserve’s departure from the [gold standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_standard "Gold standard") in 1971, which many argue has contributed to long-term inflationary pressures and a devaluation of the U.S. dollar. Ron Paul believes the Fed should be [abolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_the_Fed "End the Fed") and replaced with a return to the [gold standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_standard "Gold standard").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-:1-28) Advocates of [Austrian economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_school_of_economics "Austrian school of economics"), such as [Ludwig von Mises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises "Ludwig von Mises") and [Murray Rothbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murray_Rothbard "Murray Rothbard"), believe that the move to fiat currency destabilized the monetary system and undermined financial stability.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-181) The Federal Reserve’s handling of the [2008 financial crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis") has also been a focal point of criticism, with some arguing that the Fed’s response—[bailing out large banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_Economic_Stabilization_Act_of_2008 "Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of 2008") and financial institutions—created [moral hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_hazard "Moral hazard") and worsened the economic collapse.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-182)

During [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), the Federal Reserve's policies such as increasing its [bank reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_reserves "Bank reserves"), [quantitative easing (QE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantitative_easing "Quantitative easing"), and keeping interest rates near zero until March 2022 had been criticised by economists, especially [monetarists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetarism "Monetarism"), as greatly contributing to the inflation spike which peaked at a record high in half a century.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-183)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-184)[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve#cite_note-185)
